correctedCritiques.con-begotten-son-godhead-distinction: Strongest feature: The asymmetric-predicate argument pressures the Latin identity account: begottenness applies to the Son but not God as such, apparently generating strict distinction under the previously stated intrinsic-item criterion. Principal limitation: The formulation shifts among God, God as such, and Godhead without stabilizing their semantic scope, allowing the defender to distinguish personal from essential predication without conceding constituent nonidentity. Live burden: The critic must establish that predicate asymmetry entails ontological distinctness rather than relationally qualified identity, and that this distinction is a positive intrinsic item rather than opposition within one essence. Locked score: The very-strong placement reflects incisive responsiveness, qualification, and powerful reuse of the composition criterion, moderated by the unresolved inference from predicative asymmetry to composition.
correctedCritiques.con-changing-reality-epistemic-change: Strongest feature: The conditional argument joins immutability, pure actuality, and omniscience by asking whether changing truths require an omniscient knower to acquire or lose knowledge, making the epistemic tension directly relevant. Principal limitation: Its premise may conflate changes in what makes temporally indexed propositions true with intrinsic changes in the knower, despite acknowledging timeless knowledge of every temporal truth through one invariant cognitive act. Live burden: The critic must demonstrate that varying truth conditions entail corresponding intrinsic epistemic differences rather than merely changed extrinsic predications of unchanged comprehensive knowledge. Locked score: The very-strong placement reflects excellent structure, burden contact, explicit qualification, and evidential framing, while recognizing that the inference from changing reality to intrinsic cognitive change remains disputable.
